subthemes.text:
ANALYSIS

[7] Section 98 of the IRPA requires the RPD and RAD to reject a refugee protection claim by any person referred to in Articles 1E or 1F of the Refugee Convention. Article 1F(b) of the Convention provides that a person is excluded from the protection of the Convention if there are serious reasons for considering that they have "committed a serious non-political crime outside the country of refuge prior to his admission to that country as a refugee".

[8] The Minister bears the onus of proving that a claimant is excluded from refugee protection under Article 1F(b) of the Convention. The Minister does not have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the claimant is guilty of a crime. Rather, the standard of proof is one of "serious reasons for considering" that the claimant has committed a serious non-political crime. A crime generally will be considered as serious where a maximum sentence of 10 years or more could have been imposed had the crime been committed in Canada. However, this is a rebuttable presumption. In Febles, the Supreme Court of Canada cautioned against the use of mechanistic and decontextualized analysis that fails to take into consideration a crime's sentencing range. The Court found that, when a Criminal Code provision has a wide sentencing range, a claimant whose crime would fall at the lower end of the sentencing range should not be presumptively excluded from protection.2

[9] In Jayasekara, the Federal Court of Appeal found that, when assessing the seriousness of a crime, it is necessary to consider the elements of the crime, the mode of prosecution, the penalty prescribed, the facts, and the mitigating and aggravating circumstances underlying the conviction.3

[10] While not exhaustive, the Supreme Court has provided as examples of serious crimes homicide, rape, child molestation, wounding, arson, drug trafficking and armed robbery and noted that, even when dealing with such crimes, the presumption of seriousness may be rebutted in a particular case.4 The courts have also found that the seriousness of a crime is not to be balanced against factors extraneous to the crime or matters that occurred after the commission of the crim such as present or future danger to the host society, post-crime rehabilitation or expiation, or the risk of persecution in the country of origin.5 A claimant need not have been charged or convicted of a criminal act in order to the RPD or RAD to find that there are serious reasons for considering that the claimant committed it.6

He and XXXX both testified that he had asked her how old she was four times and she told him she was 18. He undertook no further steps to ascertain her age. XXXX XXXX XXXX was not charged in the Ukraine.

[12] The relevant crimes in Canada would be the offences of sexual interference under s. 151 of the Criminal Code and sexual assault under s. 271 of the Criminal Code.

[23] The elements of the crime in this case involve sexual intercourse with a person who has not consented or has not reached the age at which they can legally consent to the sexual activity. As noted by the RPD, the legal age of consent for sexual activity in both Ukraine and Canada is 16 years old. For the reasons set out above, I agree with the RPD's finding that XXXX XXXX XXXX did not take all reasonable steps to confirm that XXXX was at least 16 years of age. Therefore, there are serious reasons for considering that XXXX XXXX XXXX conduct would fulfill all of the required elements for the crimes of sexual interference and sexual assault.

[24] As noted by the RPD, Canadian law treats sexual interference as a serious crime. Justice Shore in Raina listed five elements of the crime that militate in favour of considering it a serious crime:
First, sexual interference affects the sexual integrity of victims under the age of 16 years; Canada considers it an abhorrent crime (R v Oldford, 2009 NLTD 124, 288 Nfld & PEIR 203 at para 13). Second, as sexual interference is serious criminality pursuant to subsection 36(1) of the IRPA. Third, even if the offence is tried by way of summary conviction, it is still considered to be a serious offence. The maximum term of imprisonment if someone is prosecuted by way of summary conviction is eighteen months which is three times the punishment for all other summary offences (Criminal Code, at 787(1)). Fourth, unlike the vast majority of offences in the Criminal Code, section 151 imposes a minimum term of imprisonment. Finally, sexual interference is a designated offence for the purpose of the forensic DNA data bank.9

[25] All of the elements of the offences of sexual interference as well as sexual assault militate in favour of a finding that the offences constitute serious crimes.

Conclusion on application of Jayasekara factors

[36] I do not agree with Counsel's argument that XXXX XXXX XXXX was only guilty of an "error in judgment" and her reference to the sexual interference in this case as a "technical "crime"". On the contrary Canadian law considers sexual interference and sexual assault to be serious crimes. Even when the two mitigating circumstances correctly accepted by the RPD are taken into account, there remain serious reasons for considering that XXXX XXXX XXXX committed a serious non-political crime. My conclusion is not altered by the text of the UNHCR handbook quoted by Counsel in the concluding section of her memorandum. I would note that parts of the narrow application of Article 1F(b) advocated by the UNHCR have not been accepted by courts in Canada. There is simply no basis in Canadian law to limit the application of Article 1F(b) to "heinous" crimes by criminals who pose a danger to Canada, as argued by Counsel.

[37] I do accept Counsel's point that there is no evidence that XXXX XXXX XXXX is anything other than a loving husband or father. However, this factor is extraneous to the offence and therefore, pursuant to the case law discussed above, must not be considered. In my view, this factor is substantially similar to the expressions of regret and redeeming post-crime conduct that the Supreme Court rejected as relevant factors for the Article 1F(b) analysis in Febles. For all the reasons set out above, I find that the RPD was correct to conclude that there are serious reasons for considering that that XXXX XXXX XXXX committed a serious non-political crime and, thus, that he is excluded from refugee protection by the combined effect of Article 1F(b) of the refugee convention and s. 98 of the IRPA.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW
[1] I dismiss this appeal for the reasons that follow.

[2] XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Ukraine who was a citizen of Nigeria by birth but renounced his Nigerian citizenship in order to become a naturalized citizen of Ukraine. XXXX XXXX XXXX met his wife, XXXX, when he was renting a room in the three-bedroom apartment owned by XXXX parents. The couple developed a relationship and had sexual intercourse which led XXXX to become pregnant. XXXX was 13 at the time. XXXX XXXX XXXXand XXXX got married a few years later and had three more children. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and their children left Ukraine to come to Canada in XXXX 2016. They all filed a claim for refugee protection at the same time, alleging a fear of anti-Black racist violence in Ukraine based on XXXX XXXX XXXX race and the family's being of mixed race. XXXX XXXX XXXX also claimed to fear persecution in both Ukraine and Nigeria on the basis of alleged bisexuality.

[3] The Minister intervened in the case to argue that XXXX XXXX XXXX should be excluded from refugee protection under Article 1F(b) of the refugee Convention. The Minister argued that there were serious reasons for considering that XXXX XXXX XXXX had committed a serious non-political crime. The Minister argued that XXXX XXXX XXXX sexual intercourse with XXXX when she was 13 years old would constitute sexual interference or sexual assault under the Criminal Code of Canada.

[4] The RPD accepted the claims filed by XXXX XXXX XXXX wife XXXX and their children. However, it found that XXXX XXXX XXXX was excluded by the combined effect of Article 1F(b) of the refugee Convention and s. 98 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). XXXX XXXX XXXX challenges the RPD's finding regarding his claim.
DECISION

[5] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1 I do not agree with any of the arguments made by the Appellant's counsel as to why she believes the RPD erred in this case. I find that the RPD was correct to conclude that XXXX XXXX XXXX is excluded from refugee protection by virtue of the combined effect of Article 1F(b) of the refugee Convention and s. 98 of the IRPA.
Proposed new evidence

[6] XXXX XXXX XXXX counsel filed an affidavit sworn by XXXX XXXX XXXX in which he restates the evidence he gave and makes arguments regarding the errors he believes the RPD made in its decision. This affidavit does not appear to have been submitted as new evidence as XXXX XXXX XXXX says in his affidavit that he is not seeking to rely on new evidence. If I am wrong and the affidavit was submitted as new evidence, it is not admissible as such as it does not meet the conditions set out in s. 110(4) of the IRPA as it simply repeats evidence that was before the RPD and makes legal argument.
ANALYSIS

[7] Section 98 of the IRPA requires the RPD and RAD to reject a refugee protection claim by any person referred to in Articles 1E or 1F of the Refugee Convention. Article 1F(b) of the Convention provides that a person is excluded from the protection of the Convention if there are serious reasons for considering that they have "committed a serious non-political crime outside the country of refuge prior to his admission to that country as a refugee".

[8] The Minister bears the onus of proving that a claimant is excluded from refugee protection under Article 1F(b) of the Convention. The Minister does not have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the claimant is guilty of a crime. Rather, the standard of proof is one of "serious reasons for considering" that the claimant has committed a serious non-political crime. A crime generally will be considered as serious where a maximum sentence of 10 years or more could have been imposed had the crime been committed in Canada. However, this is a rebuttable presumption. In Febles, the Supreme Court of Canada cautioned against the use of mechanistic and decontextualized analysis that fails to take into consideration a crime's sentencing range. The Court found that, when a Criminal Code provision has a wide sentencing range, a claimant whose crime would fall at the lower end of the sentencing range should not be presumptively excluded from protection.2

[9] In Jayasekara, the Federal Court of Appeal found that, when assessing the seriousness of a crime, it is necessary to consider the elements of the crime, the mode of prosecution, the penalty prescribed, the facts, and the mitigating and aggravating circumstances underlying the conviction.3

[10] While not exhaustive, the Supreme Court has provided as examples of serious crimes homicide, rape, child molestation, wounding, arson, drug trafficking and armed robbery and noted that, even when dealing with such crimes, the presumption of seriousness may be rebutted in a particular case.4 The courts have also found that the seriousness of a crime is not to be balanced against factors extraneous to the crime or matters that occurred after the commission of the crim such as present or future danger to the host society, post-crime rehabilitation or expiation, or the risk of persecution in the country of origin.5 A claimant need not have been charged or convicted of a criminal act in order to the RPD or RAD to find that there are serious reasons for considering that the claimant committed it.6
Factual background

[11] The relevant factual background is largely not in dispute. It is not disputed that XXXX XXXX XXXX had sexual intercourse with XXXX when she was 13 years old, leading her to become pregnant at the age of 14. He and XXXX both testified that he had asked her how old she was four times and she told him she was 18. He undertook no further steps to ascertain her age. XXXX XXXX XXXX was not charged in the Ukraine.
Legal background
[12] The relevant crimes in Canada would be the offences of sexual interference under s. 151 of the Criminal Code and sexual assault under s. 271 of the Criminal Code.

[13] Section 151 of the Criminal Code defines sexual interference as follows:
Every person who, for a sexual purpose, touches, directly or indirectly, with a part of the body or with an object, any part of the body of a person under the age of 16 years
(a) is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for a term of not more than 14 years and to a minimum punishment of imprisonment for a term of one year; or is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction and is liable to imprisonment for a term of not more than two years less a day and to a minimum punishment or imprisonment for a term of 90 days.

[14] Section 271 of the Criminal Code defines sexual assault as any touching or another person without their consent where the touching is of a sexual nature, or where the sexual integrity of the alleged victim is violated.

[15] The defence of consent is not available for these crimes if the complainant is under 16 years of age.7 There are certain exceptions to this rule if the accused and complainant are close in age but they do not apply here as XXXX XXXX XXXX was 29 at the time that he commenced having sexual intercourse with XXXX. It is not a defence that the accused believed that the complainant was 16 years of age or more at the time the offence is alleged to have been committed unless the accused took "all reasonable steps" to ascertain the age of the complainant.8

[16] This case largely turns largely on two issues: (1) whether XXXX XXXX XXXX would have been able to make out the defence of mistaken belief that XXXX was at least 16 years of age, which turns on whether he took "all reasonable steps" to ascertain her age before having sexual relations with her and (2) the balancing of the Jayasekara factors in the circumstances of this case.
Defence of belief regarding age
[17] I do not agree with Counsel that the RPD erred in finding that XXXX XXXX XXXX had not taken all reasonable steps to ascertain XXXX age before having sexual intercourse with her.

[18] Counsel argues that XXXX XXXX XXXX took reasonable steps by asking XXXX her age multiple times. Even if these were reasonable steps, the issue is whether XXXX XXXX XXXX took "all reasonable steps" to ascertain her age. I do not agree with Counsel that it was reasonable for XXXX XXXX XXXX to believe XXXX because she was very respectful and she carried out household chores, shopping and cooking. I disagree with Counsel that being very respectful is not the demeanour of a 13-year-old. I also do not agree with Counsel that household chores, shopping, and cooking are not the responsibilities of a 13-year-old. In my view, these responsibilities may well be the responsibilities of a 13-year-old who is the only girl in a household with two brothers.

[19] I agree with the RPD that considering that since XXXX XXXX XXXXand XXXX lived in close proximity in a three-bedroom apartment for approximately a year, it is reasonable to expect that XXXX XXXX XXXX knew, ought to have known, or at the very least suspected, that XXXX was under the age of 16. For example, XXXX testified to having been in eighth grade at school at the time that she and XXXX XXXX XXXX began having sexual intercourse. It may well be, as argued by Counsel, that one does not necessarily know all of the business of their co-tenants just because they live with them. However, in my view, the fact that XXXX was still in school would have been observable to XXXX XXXX XXXX, on a balance of probabilities, and it reasonably should have caused him to make further inquiries as to whether she was in fact at least 16 years of age.

[20] I also do not agree with Counsel that the RPD erred in finding that it would have been reasonable to expect XXXX XXXX XXXX to take additional steps to confirm XXXX age. I disagree with Counsel that the fact that XXXX XXXX XXXX was a vulnerable young man living in a discriminatory society and a household with XXXX brothers who hated him has any relevance to whether he took all reasonable steps to ascertain XXXX age. XXXX XXXX XXXX testified that he got along with XXXX parents; therefore, he could reasonably have determined her age from them. Likewise, the fact that XXXX XXXX XXXX had trouble finding housing as a Black man or his determination to keep his relationship with XXXX secret does not explain his failure to take what would have been basic reasonable steps to determine her age.

[21] For all these reasons, I do not accept any of Counsel's arguments as to why she believes the RPD erred in finding that XXXX XXXX XXXX had not taken all reasonable steps to determine XXXX age before having sexual intercourse with her.
Jayasekara factors
Elements of the crime

[22] I do not agree with Counsel that the factors she listed under the heading "Fact and elements of crime" in her appeal memorandum-that is, the fact that XXXX XXXX XXXXand XXXX are still together and the general discrimination that XXXX XXXX XXXX faced in Ukraine-are properly characterized as elements of the crime in this case. If anything, they are factors that one might put forward as mitigating factors. I address below whether these factors are valid mitigating factors under the Article 1F(b) analysis.

[23] The elements of the crime in this case involve sexual intercourse with a person who has not consented or has not reached the age at which they can legally consent to the sexual activity. As noted by the RPD, the legal age of consent for sexual activity in both Ukraine and Canada is 16 years old. For the reasons set out above, I agree with the RPD's finding that XXXX XXXX XXXX did not take all reasonable steps to confirm that XXXX was at least 16 years of age. Therefore, there are serious reasons for considering that XXXX XXXX XXXX conduct would fulfill all of the required elements for the crimes of sexual interference and sexual assault.

[24] As noted by the RPD, Canadian law treats sexual interference as a serious crime. Justice Shore in Raina listed five elements of the crime that militate in favour of considering it a serious crime:
First, sexual interference affects the sexual integrity of victims under the age of 16 years; Canada considers it an abhorrent crime (R v Oldford, 2009 NLTD 124, 288 Nfld & PEIR 203 at para 13). Second, as sexual interference is serious criminality pursuant to subsection 36(1) of the IRPA. Third, even if the offence is tried by way of summary conviction, it is still considered to be a serious offence. The maximum term of imprisonment if someone is prosecuted by way of summary conviction is eighteen months which is three times the punishment for all other summary offences (Criminal Code, at 787(1)). Fourth, unlike the vast majority of offences in the Criminal Code, section 151 imposes a minimum term of imprisonment. Finally, sexual interference is a designated offence for the purpose of the forensic DNA data bank.9

[25] All of the elements of the offences of sexual interference as well as sexual assault militate in favour of a finding that the offences constitute serious crimes.
Mode of prosecution

[26] Even if I were to agree with Counsel that the mode of prosecution chosen by a foreign jurisdiction is irrelevant to the assessment of the seriousness of a crime, there was no prosecution in this case. Therefore, there was no mode of prosecution chosen by authorities in Ukraine in the sense of a choice made by authorities to proceed by summary conviction versus indictment. Counsel's argument seems to be that it is relevant that XXXX XXXX XXXX was not charged by the Ukrainian authorities. I do not agree with this argument. The case law makes it clear that Article 1F(b) may apply even if the claimant was not charged or convicted in the country where the act occurred. This point is even made in the case law cited by the Appellant in which the Federal Court noted that charges may be dismissed in foreign jurisdictions for a variety of reasons including procedural issues, etc.10 The same can be said for the failure of authorities to lay any charges.

[27] Counsel speculates that XXXX XXXX XXXX was not prosecuted by Ukrainian authorities because sexual intercourse with a 13-year-old is culturally and socially accepted in Ukraine. I disagree. Instead, I concur with the RPD that the fact that sexual intercourse with a person who is under 16 is criminalized in Ukraine is a strong indication that such conduct is not culturally or socially accepted in that country. In any event, even if the acts were culturally and socially accepted in Ukraine, it is clear from the Canadian case law that the acts are treated as a serious crime in Canada.
Penalty prescribed

[28] Counsel makes no arguments on the penalty prescribed in Canada for the offences of sexual interference and sexual assault. Like the RPD, I have taken into account the Supreme Court of Canada's caution in Febles that decision-makers must not apply the 10-year sentence rule set out in the case law in an unjust, mechanistic or decontextualized manner. As noted by the RPD, sexual interference is a hybrid offence that is punishable by a sentence ranging from 90 days to 14 years. I am also mindful that the longest prison term imposed in the decisions submitted by the Minister to the RPD was 4-9 years. In the absence of specific arguments made by the Appellants' counsel on this Jayasekara factor, it suffices for me to find that I agree with the RPD's ultimate conclusion regarding the weighing of all Jayasekara factors. Even if the crimes of sexual interference and sexual assault may not attract a prison term of 10 years in Canada in practice, the caselaw cited above makes clear that these crimes are considered to be serious crimes in Canada.11
Mitigating circumstances

[29] Counsel simply states that the RPD erroneously dismissed the mitigating circumstances that XXXX XXXX XXXX previous counsel raised at the hearing. However, she does not provide any kind of argument as to why or how the RPD erred. Given the lack of detailed argument on this point, it suffices for me to confirm that, having reviewed all of the evidence in this case, I find that the RPD was correct to reject most of the mitigating circumstances raised by Counsel at the hearing.

[30] I would note that the RPD accepted as mitigating circumstances two factors listed by Counsel in her appeal memorandum: the lack of any evidence that XXXX XXXX XXXX was under the influence of alcohol or drugs and the lack of any evidence that he has a criminal record.

[31] As for the other factors listed by Counsel: I do not agree that the circumstances of how XXXX XXXX XXXXand XXXX met and how their relationship developed constitute mitigating circumstances. I also do not agree that it is a mitigating circumstance that XXXX deliberately hid her age like a typical teenager and sought to have a relationship with XXXX XXXX XXXX. On the contrary, the possibility that XXXX might be a typical teenager who hid her age would be a reason for XXXX XXXX XXXX to conduct further reasonable inquiries into her age. As noted above, the fact that XXXX XXXX XXXX was not charged or convicted in Ukraine is not determinative and does not constitute a mitigating circumstance.

[32] As far as Counsel's argument that there was no evidence of violence such as rape aside from the "technicality of the offence", I would note that the key issue in this case is the fact that a minor is legally incapable of consenting to sexual activity such as the sexual intercourse that occurred between XXXX XXXX XXXXand XXXX. If by "technicality", Counsel is referring to the fact that XXXX testified that she was a willing participant in the sexual intercourse, this does not change the fact that she was under the age in which she was legally capable of providing consent. This is far from being a technicality. For the reasons set out above, I do not agree with Counsel's argument that the evidence establishes that sexual interference with a 13-year-old is culturally accepted in Ukraine and, therefore, I agree with the RPD's conclusion that this is not a mitigating circumstance in this case.

[33] Finally, there is what is perhaps Counsel's strongest argument and that is the fact that XXXX XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX are still together. They got married a few years after her pregnancy and have been married for approximately 19 years. They have also had three other children. These circumstances give me pause. In my view, it is important for decision-makers not to blindly follow caselaw set down by the courts if it may not apply to the specific circumstances of the case before them. That said, the case law is clear that when determining the seriousness of the offence under Article 1F(b), decision-makers must not balance factors that are extraneous to, or occurred after, the commission of the criminal act being considered.12 Only factors related to the commission of the criminal offences can be considered, and whether those offences were serious within the meaning of Article 1F(b).13 I have taken into consideration that the extraneous factors that are typically referred to in the case law are the current danger posed to society, post-crime rehabilitation or persecution in the country of origin. Nevertheless, I agree with the RPD that the fact that XXXX XXXX XXXXand XXXX ended up remaining together and having three additional children is an extraneous factor which occurred after the commission of the crime. Therefore, these factors do not alter the fact that there are serious reasons for considering that XXXX XXXX XXXX committed the offence of sexual interference or sexual assault by having sexual intercourse with XXXX when she was just 13.
Aggravating circumstances

[34] I do agree with Counsel that there was no evidence to support the finding that XXXX education was delayed and her lifestyle and career choices were altered due to her sexual intercourse with XXXX XXXX XXXX and her pregnancy. This may have been the case, but there was insufficient evidence to support the finding as the RPD did not question XXXX fully on this point. The evidence shows that XXXX completed her elementary/primary school diploma in 1998 (the year she became pregnant) and she did not study any further after the pregnancy. However, the RPD did not ask XXXX about what her life plans would have been if she had not gotten pregnant.

[35] I disagree with Counsel that the RPD erred in inferring that the increased tension in XXXX relationship with her parents was not only due to the fact that she was impregnated by a Black man, but it was instead, at least in part, due to the fact that she was impregnated at the age of 13. The RPD correctly considered this to be an aggravating circumstance as it relates to the impact on the person against whom the sexual interference was committed.
Conclusion on application of Jayasekara factors

[36] I do not agree with Counsel's argument that XXXX XXXX XXXX was only guilty of an "error in judgment" and her reference to the sexual interference in this case as a "technical "crime"". On the contrary Canadian law considers sexual interference and sexual assault to be serious crimes. Even when the two mitigating circumstances correctly accepted by the RPD are taken into account, there remain serious reasons for considering that XXXX XXXX XXXX committed a serious non-political crime. My conclusion is not altered by the text of the UNHCR handbook quoted by Counsel in the concluding section of her memorandum. I would note that parts of the narrow application of Article 1F(b) advocated by the UNHCR have not been accepted by courts in Canada. There is simply no basis in Canadian law to limit the application of Article 1F(b) to "heinous" crimes by criminals who pose a danger to Canada, as argued by Counsel.

[37] I do accept Counsel's point that there is no evidence that XXXX XXXX XXXX is anything other than a loving husband or father. However, this factor is extraneous to the offence and therefore, pursuant to the case law discussed above, must not be considered. In my view, this factor is substantially similar to the expressions of regret and redeeming post-crime conduct that the Supreme Court rejected as relevant factors for the Article 1F(b) analysis in Febles. For all the reasons set out above, I find that the RPD was correct to conclude that there are serious reasons for considering that that XXXX XXXX XXXX committed a serious non-political crime and, thus, that he is excluded from refugee protection by the combined effect of Article 1F(b) of the refugee convention and s. 98 of the IRPA.
CONCLUSION

[38] For the above reasons, I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that XXXX XXXX XXXX is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
(signed)
